questions.q: Why does df.write.parquet() produce a folder with multiple part-files instead of one single file?
options: Spark distributes work across multiple partitions, and each partition writes its own file independently, in parallel
PySpark always splits files into exactly 3 parts regardless of data size
It's a bug in PySpark that has no real explanation
Only CSV writes produce multiple files; Parquet always writes one file
questions.explain: This connects directly back to Lesson 32's distributed computing model — that's the whole point of it.

questions.q: What does the _SUCCESS file inside a write output folder indicate?
options: A marker confirming the entire write completed without errors
The actual data file containing all the rows
A log of every error encountered during the write
The schema definition for the written data
questions.explain: The real data lives in the part-*.parquet files alongside it.

questions.q: What happens if you write to a path that already exists, without specifying a mode?
options: Spark raises an error by default, refusing to silently clobber existing output
It silently overwrites the existing data with no warning
It automatically appends new files to the existing ones
It writes to a randomly generated new path instead
questions.explain: mode("overwrite") is what you'd add to deliberately replace existing output instead.

questions.q: How does writing CSV or JSON compare to writing Parquet in PySpark?
options: Same .write object and mode() pattern, just a different terminal method — mirroring spark.read.csv()/.json()/.parquet() in reverse
Writing CSV and JSON requires an entirely separate API with no relation to writing Parquet
Only Parquet supports the mode() option; CSV and JSON always overwrite automatically
CSV and JSON files cannot be written from a PySpark DataFrame at all
questions.explain: This mirrors the read side from Lessons 40-42, just in reverse.

questions.q: What's the difference between mode("overwrite") and mode("append")?
options: "overwrite" replaces existing output entirely; "append" adds new files alongside the existing ones
They are functionally identical in every case
"append" deletes existing data first, then writes new data
"overwrite" is only valid for CSV files, never Parquet
questions.explain: Both explicitly declare an intent, rather than relying on Spark's error-by-default behavior on an existing path.
